query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A warm-forging treatment at 600–700 K followed by moderate annealing (∼1 h at 773 K) will refine the microstructure of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and introduce twin networks that improve fracture resistance while preserving its magneto-/barocaloric performance at near-ambient temperatures under fields up to 2–3 T and pressures up to 1 GPa.
generation.material_initial_state: As-sintered (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with large caloric effect but prone to cracking under load.
generation.intervention: Thermomechanical processing by warm forging at 600–700 K, followed by 1 h annealing at ∼773 K.
generation.conditions: Applicable to magnetic fields up to ∼2–3 T and pressures up to ∼1 GPa near ambient temperature (∼300 K).
generation.structural_mediator: Refined grain structure and stable twin networks that impede crack propagation and maintain phase-transformation pathways.
generation.mechanism: Warm forging and moderate annealing create dense twin and grain-boundary networks, promoting dislocation storage and mitigating stress concentration while preserving the core magneto-/barocaloric transitions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved fracture toughness and compressive/tensile strength compared to the as-sintered alloy, with minimal or no loss in caloric output under cycling fields.
generation.baseline: Original as-sintered alloy displaying large caloric response but poor mechanical robustness and frequent cracking.
generation.boundary: Stable under repeated magnetic/pressure loading up to the specified field and pressure near 300 K. Performance beyond these ranges is unverified.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of caloric retention and mechanical gains is inferred from analogous multi-element alloy data; direct quantitative confirmation for this precise composition is still needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two groups of specimens from the same (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 batch: one receives the warm-forging (at 600–700 K) and subsequent 1 h annealing at 773 K, and the other is left as-sintered. Conduct standardized tensile and compressive tests, measure fracture toughness, and evaluate magneto-/barocaloric responses at 2–3 T and up to 1 GPa near 300 K.
measurements: Grain size and twin boundary density via microscopy
Magnetocaloric ΔS and ΔTad under 2–3 T
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated alloy does not exhibit measurably higher mechanical robustness (e.g., yield or fracture properties) or if its caloric effect is reduced by more than ∼10% compared to the as-sintered baseline, the hypothesis is disproven.

SignificanceBack stress hardening is usually not obvious in single-phase homogeneous grains, but can be made unusually large and sustained to large tensile strains by creating an unusually heterogeneous grain structure in single-phase alloys with low stacking fault energy (SFE), as demonstrated here for the face-centered cubic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy. The low SFE facilitates the generation of twinned nanograins and stacking faults during tensile straining, dynamically reinforcing the heterogeneity. Large uniform tensile strain can be achieved after yielding even at gigapascal stress, in the absence of heterogeneities from any second phase.Keywords: heterogeneous grain structure, ductility, medium-entropy alloy, back stress hardening AbstractDuctility, i.e., uniform strain achievable in uniaxial tension, diminishes for materials with very high yield strength. AbstractStrong and ductile materials that have high resistance to corrosion and hydrogen embrittlement are rare and yet essential for realizing safety-critical energy infrastructures, hydrogen-based industries, and transportation solutions. Here we report how we reconcile these constraints in the form of a strong and ductile CoNiV medium-entropy alloy with face-centered cubic structure. It shows high resistance to hydrogen embrittlement at ambient temperature at a strain rate of 10−4 s−1, due to its low hydrogen diffusivity and the deformation twinning that impedes crack propagation. Moreover, a dense oxide film formed on the alloy’s surface reduces the hydrogen uptake rate, and provides high corrosion resistance in dilute sulfuric acid with a corrosion current density below 7 μA cm−2. decision.trend: Early studies on multi-element alloys (e.g., CrCoNi systems) showed that dislocation-slip and deformation-twinning mechanisms can improve strength, ductility, and toughness simultaneously. Subsequent work introduced heterogenous grain structures enabling high strain hardening, boosting ductility and load-bearing capacity. Later, medium-entropy alloys further demonstrated improved mechanical robustness in hostile environments but did not address the trade-off between mechanical integrity and functional properties such as caloric performance. While these approaches successfully enhanced mechanical behavior, none directly tackled preserving magneto- or pressure-caloric performance in tandem with crack suppression, leaving the integrated magnetocaloric-mechanical optimization largely unaddressed.
decision.unsolved: How to suppress cracking and enhance mechanical load-bearing capability in high-entropy alloys formulated for magneto- or pressure-caloric applications—without sacrificing the large caloric response—remains an open design challenge. Approaches that exploit composition-based strengthening may degrade magnetic or structural phase-change properties needed for refrigeration, so a single-step operational or microstructural intervention that preserves composition is needed.
decision.lever: Warm-forge the alloy at 600–700 K to generate a stable, microstructurally refined network of twins and fine grains, followed by moderate annealing (∼1 h at 773 K) to relieve residual stress while retaining the twin substructure. Operating fields of up to 2–3 T and pressures up to 1 GPa can be applied at temperatures near ambient (∼300 K).
decision.why: Prior work on CrCoNi medium-entropy alloys (PMC5321736, PMC6048477, PMC7299985) demonstrated that twinning and heterogeneous grain structures effectively balance strength, ductility, and toughness without requiring compositional changes. A carefully tuned thermomechanical routine can refine grain size and promote twin networks that arrest cracks and accommodate stresses, sustaining mechanical integrity while preserving the intrinsic magnetocaloric effect governed primarily by alloy composition.
